巴拉圭豎琴以指甲撥弦，指甲留長；右手負責高音區，左手負責低音區，右拇指可在低音弦: The Paraguayan harp is plucked with the fingernails, which are kept long; the right hand takes the treble and the left hand the bass, the right thumb can strike the bass strings rhythmically and glide across the treble strings, and the left hand keeps the rhythm in the bass. Traditionally only the first four fingers of each hand are used, and only the new generation uses all ten. The tuning is a seven-note diatonic scale to the octave, and minor is used to express Guaraní feeling. Most pieces are not written down but passed on by ear, and the fingering is taught from teacher to pupil. Begin with the division of labour between the hands, the fingernail plucking and the rhythm.
巴拉圭豎琴以熱帶木材、松木與雪松製成，琴頭多取當地帕洛桑托木；琴身由頭、臂、共鳴: The Paraguayan harp is made of tropical woods, pine and cedar, and the neck is often of local palo santo; the body has three parts, head, arm and soundbox, and the source does not say which wood each part uses. Traditionally the strings were tightly twisted catgut; for the last fifty years they have mostly been nylon, single-strand imported nylon for the treble and double-wound nylon for the bass. The tuning pegs were once hand-carved, later guitar-style machine heads, and better instruments have levers that raise a string by a semitone.

It is played solo, in duets for two harps or with a guitar, less often with a violin, and traditionally without percussion. Modern players also take in Western styles such as the classical harp, jazz and easy listening. The national repertoire often played includes La Misionera ('The Missionary Woman'), Tren Lechero ('The Milk Train') and Pájaro Campana ('The Bell Bird'), as well as Cascada ('Waterfall') by Digno García.

Its range is wide, from the deep resonance of the bass to the crystal clarity of the treble, in clearly marked layers. The strings are nylon or gut, and plucking them gives a warm, soft tone with a natural ring trailing after it. The resonating body is cleverly shaped, so the sound projects and penetrates well and fills the room. Against the heavy splendour of the classical harp, the Paraguayan harp sounds lighter and livelier; against the guitar, it has more metallic sheen and more depth of resonance. That distinctive sound makes it one of the most recognisable instruments in South American folk music.

The Paraguayan harp is the national instrument of Paraguay, a chordophone, Hornbostel–Sachs number 322.211. It comes from the meeting of European and Guaraní musical cultures and developed from the classical angular harp; it is a diatonic harp with commonly between 32 and 46 strings, made of tropical woods, pine and cedar. The body has three parts, head, arm and body, with the central arm taking the tension and the strings passing through the middle of the head. Players keep their fingernails long, the right hand playing the treble and the left hand the bass rhythm; it can be played solo, in ensemble with another harp or a guitar, and to accompany traditional songs in Guaraní, and in the past it was mostly played by country men.
巴拉圭豎琴源自西班牙殖民時期耶穌會瓜拉尼傳教區引入的古典角形豎琴，融合歐洲與瓜拉: The Paraguayan harp derives from the classical angular harp brought in during the Spanish colonial period by the Jesuit Guaraní missions, and it fuses European and Guaraní musical cultures. The Portuguese Capuchin missions in Brazil and Uruguay once built instruments on sixteenth- and seventeenth-century Portuguese and Spanish models and exported them to Europe; in Paraguay the Franciscan missionaries had a harder time forcing the Guaraní to work, which let Guaraní culture and language survive, and the harp became a country instrument and a national symbol. After the middle of the twentieth century, male players carried it to Europe, Japan and the Middle East and took in classical, jazz and other styles; women took part in larger numbers only towards the end of the twentieth century.
